title: Collaborative Research: AF: Small: Adaptive Optimization of Stochastic and Noisy Function
contribution: NSF CCF Algorithmic Foundations award 2008434 (Cornell, PI Scheinberg, 10/2020-09/2024, $101,000 obligated). Outcomes report: adaptive step search, trust region and cubic-regularized Newton analysed under biased, bounded-irreducible, arbitrarily-corrupted (with positive probability) and biased light-tailed estimators; convergence at fast rates to a neighbourhood of stationary points with explicit neighbourhood bounds; 3 PhD students; REU on standard and robust gradient estimators that found theory-practice gaps (NSF outcomes report).
problem_entry: SG and its variants are nonadaptive and need expensive data-dependent hyperparameter tuning per task; goal is adaptive algorithms with theoretical guarantees (NSF abstract).
key_idea: Base stochastic adaptive methods on deterministic line search and trust region; since these lack optimal worst-case complexity, focus on adaptive cubic regularization, analysed through a framework viewing adaptive minimization as a renewal-reward stochastic process (NSF abstract).
positioning: Seven award publications listed: Jin-Scheinberg NeurIPS 2021; Scheinberg-Xie WSC 2023; Berahas-Cao-Choromanski-Scheinberg FoCM; Jin-Scheinberg-Xie SIOPT 2024 and Math. Program. 2024; Cao-Berahas-Scheinberg Math. Program.; Berahas-Cao-Scheinberg SIOPT 2021 (NSF record).
limits_future: Outcomes report names gaps between theory and practice found in the REU robust-gradient-estimation work as future work (NSF outcomes report).

method_links.note: Renewal-reward stochastic-process framework stated as the analytic basis in a PI-written grant abstract.
Adaptive stochastic methods built from deterministic line search, trust region and cubic regularization, motivated by avoiding hyperparameter tuning.

Report enumerates oracle failure types (bias, bounded irreducible noise, arbitrary corruption with positive probability, light tails) and states convergence to a noise-determined neighbourhood (Method 1 step 3).

title: Complexity analysis framework of adaptive optimization methods via martingales
contribution: Talk (Scholar venue 'Complexity 17' unexplained). Abstract read is that of the same-family Cornell ORIE Colloquium talk of 20 Sep 2018 ('Convergence analysis of adaptive stochastic optimization methods via martingales'); claimed results: a general framework plus stronger rates for stochastic trust region and the first stochastic line search with convergence guarantees (talk abstract).
problem_entry: A very general framework for unconstrained adaptive stochastic optimization covering line search and trust region with random models (talk abstract).
key_idea: Keep step acceptance, trust-region adjustment, second-order models and adaptive sampling; bound the expected stopping time of a stochastic process satisfying stated assumptions, then derive each method's rate by verifying that its process satisfies them (talk abstract).
positioning: Claimed results match the topics of S013 (stochastic trust region via supermartingales) and S015 (stochastic line search with expected complexity) (inferred from titles).

method_links.note: Stopping-time framework for adaptive methods stated in a talk abstract.
Framework retains the classical acceptance criterion and trust-region adjustment.

transferable: Split a complexity proof into a process-level theorem (expected stopping time under abstract assumptions on the process) and a per-algorithm lemma set verifying those assumptions, so a new algorithm needs only the verification (talk abstract).

title: Finite difference gradient approximation: To randomize or not?
contribution: Short sole-author position piece (IJOC 34(5):2384-2388, 5 pp., 12 references per Crossref) arguing that randomized finite-difference gradients have no clear advantage over classical finite differences inside optimization methods, and posing the open question of a setting where they would; names scaling of black-box methods with dimension as the larger challenge (abstract).
problem_entry: Against a trend: randomized FD schemes are popular, but it is unclear they beat classical FD when employed inside an optimization method (abstract).
key_idea: Point to theoretical and practical evidence that the opposite holds in a general optimization setting, then ask whether any particular setting shows the randomized method's advantage, at least numerically (abstract).
positioning: Crossref references include the group's FoCM 2022 comparison (S006), Nesterov-Spokoiny (FoCM), Duchi et al. (IEEE TIT 2015), Ghadimi-Lan (SIOPT 2013), Spall 1992/2000, More-Wild (TOMS 2012), Larson-Menickelly-Wild (Acta Numerica 2019), Maggiar et al. (SIOPT 2018), the Conn-Scheinberg-Vicente book, Shamir (JMLR 2017), Snoek et al. 2012 (Crossref).
writing: Question-form title; abstract closes a critique with an explicit open question rather than a verdict (abstract).
limits_future: Larger challenge named: black-box optimization methods that scale well with problem dimension (abstract); stated limits otherwise not read.

method_links.note: Estimator choice judged by performance inside the outer optimization method, not in isolation; builds on the cited FoCM comparison S006.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: close a critique with a falsifiable open question
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Position piece against randomized FD ends by asking for a setting where the new method's advantage can be shown, at least numerically.

transferable: Close a critique of a popular method with an explicit, testable open question (in which setting would it clearly win, even only numerically?) so the piece invites a counter-example instead of only dismissing the method (abstract).

quotes.text: Despite of the popularity of the latter, we argue that it is unclear whether the randomized schemes have an advantage over the traditional methods when employed inside an optimization method.
The larger underlying challenge is a development of black box optimization methods that scale well with the problem dimension.

title: Collaborative Research: AF: Small: A Unified Framework for Analyzing Adaptive Stochastic Optimization Methods Based on Probabilistic Oracles
contribution: NSF CCF award 2438005 (Georgia Tech, PI Scheinberg, 07/2024-12/2025, $108,000 obligated, listed FY 2022). Outcomes report: high-probability complexity bounds for trust-region, cubic-regularization and step-search methods with noisy/unreliable inputs; adaptive stochastic ISTA/FISTA and proximal trust region for convex composite problems; zero-one and ranking loss approximations; accelerated shuffling methods; stochastic methods for nonsmooth and constrained problems (NSF outcomes report).
problem_entry: Algorithms are launched with a prescribed trajectory, so parameters are tuned and the target is hit only after many expensive misses; assumptions are restrictive (e.g. uncorrupted data) (NSF abstract).
key_idea: Adaptive self-tuning methods with rigorous guarantees, extended to imperfect information (biased function values, corrupted data, novel objective approximations) and to constrained learning, packaged as a unified analysis framework with easy-to-use tools (NSF abstract).
positioning: Two award publications listed: Ghanbari-Li-Scheinberg (Vietnam J. Math. 2025); Nguyen-Scheinberg-Tran (JOTA 2025) (NSF record). 2024 start with FY2022 funds suggests a transferred award (inferred from dates).
limits_future: Under review per report: nonsmooth stochastic trust region, unified high-probability framework for unreliable inputs, ARC, sample complexity, stochastic SQP (NSF outcomes report).

method_links.note: Probabilistic oracles, with biased function information and corrupted data as the named extension.
Unified framework for analyzing adaptive stochastic methods; high-probability complexity bounds reported.
Adaptive variants of classical ISTA/FISTA and trust-region methods.

title: OPTIMA (identified as OPTIMA 79: Geometry in model-based algorithms for derivative-free unconstrained optimization)
contribution: Expository MPS newsletter feature (OPTIMA 79, PDF created 2009-06-02) surveying model-based DFO geometry; abstract credits Conn-Scheinberg-Vicente with the general convergence theory and Scheinberg-Toint with the self-correcting property giving convergence under very mild requirements (OPTIMA p. 1, abstract). Body not read.
problem_entry: DFO for nonlinear problems where derivatives are impractical (computational cost or numerical inaccuracy); applications: circuit tuning, aircraft configuration, water-pipe calibration, oil-reservoir modelling (OPTIMA p. 1, abstract).
key_idea: Historical framing: sampling methods until the late 1990s, then model-based trust-region DFO (Powell; Conn, Scheinberg, Toint) with linear/quadratic interpolation models; geometry question resolved via convergence theory and the self-correcting property (OPTIMA p. 1, abstract).
positioning: Credits Powell as pioneer and Conn, Scheinberg, Toint and Vicente for advances and theory (OPTIMA p. 1, abstract).

method_links.note: Scheinberg's own essay ties interpolation-set geometry to the self-correcting property and convergence under very mild requirements; supplies the article title SKILL.md lists as not retrieved. The Moré-Wild claim in SKILL.md is not checked.
